rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Arab idolaters acknowledged God as creator, owner, and controller of the heavens and earth, yet maintained polytheistic practices, doubted the Resurrection, or trusted intercessors to save them.
rows.anchor: the Idolaters of Arabia regarded God to be the creator and owner and the sole controller

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says contemporary Muslims repeat the contradiction: they acknowledge God and claim faith while rejecting its necessary consequences in belief and conduct.
rows.anchor: today’s Muslims are also inflicted with similar contradictory views.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “if you know” sarcastically exposes their contradictory belief; knowledge composed of contradictions is extreme ignorance, so they should reconsider their denial of monotheism, judgment, and the Messenger’s preaching.
rows.anchor: The words “if you know” are a type of sarcastic remark on their contradictory view.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “glorious throne” represents God’s absolute authority; the Arabs likewise regarded Him as sole authority over the universe rather than assigning separate deities to heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: “glorious throne” signifies God’s absolute authority.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If they affirm that God created heaven and earth, the Prophet asks why they do not fear Him while disrupting His order and associating partners; none can avert His punishment for disobedience.
rows.anchor: why they do not fear Him if they create disruption and disorder in His system.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word malakūt means the reins of authority.
rows.anchor: here means “the reins of authority.” The polytheists of Arabia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parables warn that disbelief ultimately destroys individual and collective life; believers should adopt faith in every sphere, while disbelievers who remain in layered darkness should contemplate their fate.
rows.anchor: ultimately it destroys the individual and collective lives of people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without belief in God and His true attributes, a person cannot understand the universe’s origin and purpose, human accountability, or good and evil, and wanders toward destruction; faith illuminates these questions and guides action along the straight path.
rows.anchor: the radiance of faith lights up everything for him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith entering the heart adds its light to the light of human nature and illuminates the inner self.
rows.anchor: the radiance of faith that enters a heart adds another light to the light of human nature

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The niche represents the human heart; when illuminated, the heart lights a person’s inner and outer self.
rows.anchor: refers to the heart of a person that has been likened to a niche where oil-lamps are placed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The crystal protects a flame from gusts, like faith stabilizes the heart in all circumstances and makes it content; the Qur’an calls such a heart the contented soul and faith’s greatest treasure.
rows.anchor: It is such a heart which the Qur’ā n (89:27) has referred to as the “contented soul”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A shining, clean crystal transmits light, while a dirty one obstructs it; faith cleanses the heart and makes it shine like a mirror.
rows.anchor: the light of faith cleanses the heart from all kinds of filth and makes it shine like a mirror.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “blessed” describes a fruit-bearing tree, just as the Qur’an also calls lush, fertile land blessed.
rows.anchor: similarly here a tree which bears fruit is called “blessed.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The olive tree stands in the orchard’s center, protected from the harsher sun and wind at its borders; this signifies its exceptional luxuriance.
rows.anchor: This tree is right in the middle of an orchard, neither from its eastern side not western one.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Oil so clear it seems to kindle without fire signifies faith taking root in pure, unperverted nature and igniting at the weakest stimulus, adding faith’s light to natural light.
rows.anchor: faith takes its roots in the chests of those people whose nature is pure and free of any perversion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When yahdī takes the preposition lām, it also carries the sense of granting an urge, as explained in the commentary on 10:35.
rows.anchor: it also encompasses the meaning of “being granted urge”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s established practice is to grant faith’s light to those who preserve the light of their nature; those who corrupt or lose it through deviation and misdeeds do not receive faith’s light.
rows.anchor: Only those people are provided this light of faith who preserve the light of their nature and keep it pure.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The east-west wording also alludes to Jewish-Christian dispute over the House of God: their departure from the middle left them without the title of the middle nation and unable to embrace Islam.
rows.anchor: subtle insinuation found in these words regarding the dispute between the Jews and Christians

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives further urge toward truth only to those who value the urge already given; those who fail to do so lose their innate guidance.
rows.anchor: God provides further urge to accept the truth to only those who duly value the urge they already have.

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus is reported to say that someone untrustworthy with a penny will not be entrusted with a hundred thousand, illustrating why squandered initial guidance does not merit further urging.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) is reported to have said: “if a person is a thief in one penny

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A governing noun is omitted before “for people”; the implied sense is that God states the parables to educate and remind people to value faith and illuminate their hearts.
rows.anchor: A governing noun is suppressed before

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parables are the highest and most effective way to explain realities; people’s failure to benefit from them is their misfortune.
rows.anchor: Parables are the highest and the most effective means to explain realities.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God acts with knowledge and wisdom, knows every person’s inner and outer self, and deals with each according to what they merit.
rows.anchor: God’s intent is always based on His knowledge and wisdom.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “in houses” is grammatically connected to “niche.”
rows.anchor: in houses) are related to

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These are places of worship, not idol-worship or liquor-drinking venues; the lamp signifies an upright believer’s heart, which is found among believers in God’s mosques.
rows.anchor: This niche is found in places where God is worshipped.

rows.speaker: Al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī prefers connecting “in houses” with the niche, reading the verse as locating these illuminated believers in mosques.
rows.anchor: Al-Zamakhshar ī has given preference to this view.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb rafaʿa here means to build or construct, as in the account of Abraham building the foundations of the House.
rows.anchor: here means to build and construct. A similar usage of this word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr includes prayer and every other form of remembrance of God, including acts undertaken to raise the banner of His religion.
rows.anchor: encompasses the prayer as well all other forms of God’s remembrance
